"'''I Love Rock 'n' Roll'''" is a 1975 rock song written by [[Alan Merrill]] and [[Jake Hooker (musician)|Jake Hooker]] for their English [[glam rock]] band, the [[Arrows (British band)|Arrows]]. The song received international attention when it was covered by [[Joan Jett]] for her 1981 album [[I Love Rock 'n Roll (album)|''I Love Rock 'n Roll'']]. Jett's version is the best known rendition of the song.

Conceived by Merrill in response to "[[It's Only Rock 'n Roll (But I Like It)]]" by [[the Rolling Stones]], Jett first saw the Arrows perform the song on [[Arrows (TV series)|their self-titled UK series]] in 1976. She brought it to her band of the time, [[the Runaways]], who ultimately passed on the song. After the Runaways split, Jett and the Blackhearts covered the song. Released in 1982 as a single, it topped the U.S. [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] for seven weeks and several international charts, and was [[RIAA certification|certified platinum]] by the [[Recording Industry Association of America]] (RIAA) for selling over two million copies within the United States.

Jett's version is often featured in professional listings of the greatest songs of all time. It is an enduring work, being covered by artists such as [[Britney Spears]] and parodied by [["Weird Al" Yankovic]]. In 2016, it was inducted into the [[Grammy Hall of Fame]].

sections.heading: Background
sections.wikitext:
[[Joan Jett]] saw the [[Arrows (British band)|Arrows]] perform "I Love Rock 'n' Roll" on their weekly UK television series ''[[Arrows (TV series)|Arrows]]'' while she was touring England with [[the Runaways]] in 1976.<ref name="Record8">{{cite magazine |last=Gross |first=Jonathan |date=June 1983 |title=Joan Jett: The Road Goes On Forever |magazine=[[The Record (magazine)|The Record]] |location=Toronto |pages=1, 10–11, 30 |volume=2 |issue=8}}</ref> The Runaways' producer and manager [[Kim Fowley]] had the band learn the song in the summer of 1977, during the brief period when [[Victory Tischler-Blue|Vicki Blue]] had replaced [[Jackie Fox]] as bass player and [[Cherie Currie]] was still the group's vocalist.<ref name="KF_RBP_Sounds_8-6-1977">{{cite journal |last1=Robertson |first1=Sandy |title=Kim Fowley: The Dorian Gray of Rock'n'Roll |journal=Sounds |date=6 August 1977 |url=https://www.rocksbackpages.com/Library/Article/kim-fowley-the-dorian-gray-of-rocknroll |access-date=15 September 2023 |publisher=United Newspapers |location=London |format=Online |url-access=subscription}}</ref> However, the band ultimately passed on the song since they had previously covered [[The Velvet Underground]]'s "[[Rock & Roll (The Velvet Underground song)|Rock & Roll]]".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Burditt |first=Peter |date=April 17, 2025 |title=The Band That Almost Permanently Halted the Creation of Joan Jett's "I Love Rock 'n' Roll" |url=https://americansongwriter.com/the-band-that-almost-permanently-halted-the-creation-of-joan-jetts-i-love-rock-n-roll/ |access-date=June 25, 2025 |website=[[American Songwriter]] |language=en-US}}</ref> After the Runaways disbanded, Jett recorded the first version of the song in 1979, with [[Steve Jones (musician)|Steve Jones]] and [[Paul Cook]] of [[Sex Pistols]]. It was released on vinyl in 1979 on [[Vertigo Records]] as a B-side to "[[You Don't Own Me]]" to limited success. 

In 1981, Jett re-recorded the song with her newly-founded band, [[the Blackhearts]],<ref name="Cover song" /> to be featured on the [[I Love Rock 'n Roll (album)|album of the same name]]. Jett recalled the recording being vigorously paced, since, "During the weekdays we'd be in the studio and during the weekends we'd travel around the New York area, the Northeast, doing gigs, [...] we were doing both without really stopping. Which was good I thought, it really kept us together, it kept us sharp."<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Lababedi |first=Iman |date=June 1982 |title=Joan Jett Is A Very Nice Girl |url=https://www.rocksbackpages.com/Library/Article/joan-jett-is-a-very-nice-girl |url-access=subscription |access-date=June 14, 2019 |magazine=[[Creem]] |location=Detroit |via=[[Rock's Backpages]]}}</ref> It was produced by [[Kenny Laguna]], Jett's long-time friend and collaborator, and [[Ritchie Cordell]]. Like the Arrows' original version, it is a hard rock song.<ref>{{cite web |last=Huey |first=Steve |title=I Love Rock N' Roll – Song Review |url=https://www.allmusic.com/song/i-love-rock-n-roll-mt0010368331 |access-date=20 February 2014 |work=[[AllMusic]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Talevski |first=Nick |title=Rock Obituaries – Knocking on Heaven's Door |publisher=[[Music Sales Group|Omnibus Press]] |year=2006 |isbn=978-1-8460-9091-2 |page=100 |quote=Cordell joined [[Kenny Laguna]], his former session player and then manager of Joan Jett & the Blackhearts, to co-produce the group's chart-topping hard-rock anthem 'I Love Rock 'N Roll'.}}</ref>

Of the song's impact compared to the Arrows' original recording, Dave Ling of [[Classic Rock (magazine)|''Louder'']] quipped that "you'd be forgiven for not knowing it was a cover version." Arrow band member Alan Merrill himself told Jett in 2013 that "she was an honorary Arrow because she looked like one of us. I always fancied her, and we developed a loose friendship. Since then she has played a large part in my life and I in hers, whether she admits it or not."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ling |first=Dave |date=March 31, 2022 |title=The complicated journey of the song that catapulted Joan Jett towards stardom |url=https://www.loudersound.com/features/the-complicated-journey-of-the-song-that-catapulted-joan-jett-towards-stardom |access-date=June 25, 2025 |website=[[Classic Rock (magazine)|Louder]] |language=en}}</ref>

Joan Jett saw the Arrows perform "I Love Rock 'n' Roll" on their weekly UK television series Arrows while she was touring England with the Runaways in 1976. The Runaways' producer and manager Kim Fowley had the band learn the song in the summer of 1977, during the brief period when Vicki Blue had replaced Jackie Fox as bass player and Cherie Currie was still the group's vocalist. However, the band ultimately passed on the song since they had previously covered The Velvet Underground's "Rock & Roll". After the Runaways disbanded, Jett recorded the first version of the song in 1979, with Steve Jones and Paul Cook of Sex Pistols. It was released on vinyl in 1979 on Vertigo Records as a B-side to "You Don't Own Me" to limited success. 

In 1981, Jett re-recorded the song with her newly-founded band, the Blackhearts, to be featured on the album of the same name. Jett recalled the recording being vigorously paced, since, "During the weekdays we'd be in the studio and during the weekends we'd travel around the New York area, the Northeast, doing gigs, [...] we were doing both without really stopping. Which was good I thought, it really kept us together, it kept us sharp." It was produced by Kenny Laguna, Jett's long-time friend and collaborator, and Ritchie Cordell. Like the Arrows' original version, it is a hard rock song.

Of the song's impact compared to the Arrows' original recording, Dave Ling of Louder quipped that "you'd be forgiven for not knowing it was a cover version." Arrow band member Alan Merrill himself told Jett in 2013 that "she was an honorary Arrow because she looked like one of us. I always fancied her, and we developed a loose friendship. Since then she has played a large part in my life and I in hers, whether she admits it or not."

sections.heading: Release and promotion
sections.wikitext:
"I Love Rock 'n Roll" was released as a [[Single (music)|single]] on January 20, 1982, distributed by [[Boardwalk Records]] in the United States and Canada.

The music video for "I Love Rock 'n Roll" produced by Barry Ralbag, received heavy play by the fledgling [[MTV]] network. It featured Jett and the Blackhearts traveling to a small, dingy bar and then exciting the drunken crowd by performing the song and yelling out its [[refrain|chorus]]. The filming location was at the corner of Lexington Avenue and East 85th Street on the Upper East Side in Manhattan, New York City. At the time, the bar was called Privates, now a Starbucks. A snippet of Jett's 1981 hit "[[Bad Reputation (Joan Jett song)|Bad Reputation]]" can be heard at the beginning of the video. The video was originally in colour, but it was converted to black and white because Jett hated the look of her red leather jumpsuit.<ref>{{Citation |title=Joan Jett & the Blackhearts: I Love Rock 'n Roll (Video 1982) |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt6973600/trivia |access-date=22 December 2018}}</ref>

In 1993 Joan Jett & the Blackhearts made another music video for the song as part of the ''[[Wayne's World 2]]'' soundtrack. The video consisted of scenes from the movie, with [[Mike Myers (actor)|Mike Myers]] and [[Dana Carvey]], mixed with footage of Jett and her band in a faux concert filmed at [[Irving Plaza]] in New York City. The song was again released as a single by Warner/Reprise with "Activity Grrrl" as the B-side.<ref>{{Cite web |year=1994 |title=Joan Jett and the Blackhearts* – I Love Rock & Roll |url=https://www.discogs.com/Joan-Jett-And-The-Blackhearts-I-Love-Rock-Roll/master/717326 |access-date=22 December 2018 |website=Discogs |language=en}}</ref>

sections.heading: Reception and legacy
sections.wikitext:
"I Love Rock 'n Roll" was a critical and commercial success. At the [[Juno Awards of 1983]], the song was nominated for [[Juno Award for Best Selling Single|International Single of the Year]], losing to "[[Eye of the Tiger]]" by [[Survivor (band)|Survivor]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Past Nominees + Winners |url=https://junoawards.ca/awards/past-winners-nominees/ |access-date=2024-11-21 |website=The JUNO Awards |language=en-US}}</ref> The song became a [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] number-one single for seven weeks, being the only one for the band.<ref>[[Joel Whitburn|Whitburn, Joel]] (2004). ''The Billboard Book of Top 40 Hits'', 8th Edition (Billboard Publications), page 322.</ref> On September 20, 1982, the song was [[RIAA certification|platinum-certified]] by the [[Recording Industry Association of America]] (RIAA) for selling over two million copies in the United States.<ref>{{Cite certification|region=United States|title=|artist=Joan Jett & the Blackhearts|type=|access-date=June 25, 2025}}</ref> It ultimately emerged as both the [[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1982|third most successful song of 1982]] and one of the decade's most successful songs.<ref>{{cite web |last=Cad |first=Saint |date=14 October 2012 |title=10 More Famous Songs With Unknown Originals |url=http://listverse.com/2012/10/14/10-more-famous-songs-with-unknown-originals/ |access-date=21 June 2013 |work=Listverse}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Sheffield |first=Rob |date=November 23, 2023 |title=Joan Jett, 'I Love Rock & Roll' |url=https://au.rollingstone.com/music/music-lists/-52935/joan-jett-i-love-rock-roll-53039/ |access-date=June 25, 2025 |website=[[Rolling Stone Australia]] |language=en-AU}}</ref> In 2024, 42 years after its release, it debuted on the [[Billboard (magazine)|''Billboard'']] Hard Rock Streaming Songs charts at number 23.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=McIntyre |first=Hugh |date=June 17, 2024 |title=Joan Jett's 'I Love Rock 'N' Roll' Debuts On A Billboard Chart Decades After It Became A Classic |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/hughmcintyre/2024/06/17/joan-jetts-i-love-rock-n-roll-debuts-on-a-billboard-chart-decades-after-it-became-a-classic/ |access-date=June 25, 2025 |website=[[Forbes]] |language=en}}</ref>

[[AllMusic]]'s Steve Huey called the song a "cornerstone single in the brave new world opened up for female rock musicians" and said her cover "gives the tune a slightly punky flavor—sort of the [[Ramones]] meets "[[Louie Louie]]"—but the song's deliberate tempo and Jett's love of the big chorus hook set it squarely in the realm of hard rock."<ref>{{Citation |last=Huey |first=Steve |title=I Love Rock N' Roll - Joan Jett & the Blackhearts |url=https://www.allmusic.com/song/i-love-rock-n-roll-mt0013578389 |access-date=June 25, 2025 |publisher=[[AllMusic]] |language=en}}</ref> Michael Cohen of ''[[Creem]]'' complimented Jett's "contagious enthusiasm".<ref name="Cohen">{{cite magazine |last=Cohen |first=Mitchell |date=March 1982 |title=Joan Jett: I Love Rock 'N' Roll (Boardwalk) |url=https://www.rocksbackpages.com/Library/Article/joan-jett-ii-love-rock-n-roll-iboardwalk |url-access=subscription |access-date=November 1, 2018 |magazine=[[Creem]] |location=Detroit |via=[[Rock's Backpages]]}}</ref> Hugh McIntyre of ''[[Forbes]]'' deemed it "one of the world’s favorite rock songs. Writers of Record World said it "has anthem qualities and heroic lead guitar riffs that should take it all the way to the top." Tom Breihan of Stereogum wrote, "Joan Jett uses the song to put the full force of her tough-kid charisma on display. She makes a simple statement of musical preference sound like a rallying cry, a statement of religious truth, a come-on. She makes rock ‘n’ roll sound like something worth loving."

In 2005, Q placed "I Love Rock 'n Roll" at number 85 on their list of the "100 Greatest Guitar Tracks Ever!" In 2008, the song was placed at number 56 in Billboard{{'}}s "Greatest Songs of All Time" list. Rolling Stone has placed the song on the 2004 and 2010 iterations of their "500 Greatest Songs of All Time" list, at 484 and 491 respectively; the same publication also ranked it number 97 on their 2023 list of "The 200 Best Songs of The 1980s". Jett's version was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2016.

sections.heading: Background and release
sections.wikitext: "I Love Rock 'n' Roll" is the fourth European single from American singer [[Britney Spears]]' third studio album, ''[[Britney (album)|Britney]]'' (2001), released on 27 May 2002. The song was used in her 2002 film ''[[Crossroads (2002 film)|Crossroads]]'', in which her character Lucy performs it in a karaoke bar. Spears said of the song, "They asked me to sing karaoke in the movie ''Crossroads'' and I've actually sung 'I Love Rock 'n' Roll' in a lot of clubs that I've been to."<ref>{{cite news|last=Dingwall|first=John|title=OTR..Off the Record: Your Time Is Up, Jacko; Britney Wants Album Top Slot|newspaper=[[Daily Record (Scotland)|Daily Record]]|date=5 November 2001|page=19}}</ref> Spears has publicly stated that the original song is one of her favorites. She listened to the original Arrows Mickie Most-produced version just before she recorded the song, according to [[Jive Records|Jive]] A&R representative Steve Lunt. The scratches performed on this version were performed by Corey Chase at The Hit Factory Criteria studios in Miami. When promoting the single's release, Spears mistakenly attributed the successful version of the song to [[Pat Benatar]] instead of Joan Jett.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.suntimes.com/output/rock/sho-sunday-britney04.html|title=What Britney said, or should have|first=Jim|last=DeRogatis|date=4 November 2001|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20011116135611/http://www.suntimes.com/output/rock/sho-sunday-britney04.html|archive-date=16 November 2001|newspaper=[[Chicago Sun-Times]]|access-date=26 February 2012|author-link=Jim DeRogatis|url-status=dead}}</ref>

sections.heading: Promotion
sections.wikitext:
The music video, directed by [[Chris Applebaum]], shows Spears with her own band, a stack of speakers and flashing lights. The video begins in black and white and switches to and from colour throughout. It was shot at The Inn, a bar in Long Beach, New York. The video was ranked at number two on the 100 Best Videos of 2002 list during [[MTV Latin America]]'s countdown. A director's cut version of the video was later leaked, containing previously unseen scenes. 

The song was performed live during Spears' [[Dream Within a Dream Tour]] (2001–02). In 2016, it was added to the revamped set list of her [[Las Vegas]] residency show, [[Britney: Piece of Me]] (2016–17), marking the first time Spears performed the song in 14 years. During the performance, Spears rode a mechanical electric guitar, which simulated a mechanical bull, as it rotated on stage. The same prop electric guitar had been used during her [[Femme Fatale Tour]] (2011) for a segment in which she covered the song "[[Burning Up (Madonna song)|Burning Up]]" by [[Madonna (entertainer)|Madonna]]. At the [[2016 Billboard Music Awards|2016 ''Billboard'' Music Awards]], the song was performed as part of a medley.

sections.heading: Reception
sections.wikitext:
"I Love Rock 'n' Roll" charted moderately upon release, reaching the top 20 in most regions. The song was moderately successful in the UK, where it peaked at number 13 (which, at the time, was Spears' lowest peak for a single released there, until "[[If U Seek Amy]]" only managed to reach number 20 in 2009). It was certified gold in Australia.

Spears' cover was met with mostly favorable reviews. ''[[NME]]''{{'}}s Ted Kessler wrote that she "still works best when making a good pop cheese and dance sandwich: there's the ace [[Rodney Jerkins]]-produced version of [[Joan Jett]]'s 'I Love Rock 'n' Roll', which does exactly what it says on the tin."<ref>{{cite news|last=Kessler|first=Ted|title=Britney Spears : Britney|url=https://www.nme.com/reviews/reviews-nme-5783-338289|access-date=17 April 2022|newspaper=[[NME]]|date=30 October 2001}}</ref> ''[[Rolling Stone]]''{{'}}s Barry Walters wrote that "producer Rodney Jerkins' hip-hop blaspheming of Joan Jett's "I Love Rock 'n' Roll" doesn't go as far as it should (is a [[Limp Bizkit]] remix in its future?), but it certainly beats what her earlier studio architects did to those [[Sonny and Cher]] ("[[The Beat Goes On (Sonny & Cher song)|The Beat Goes On]]" on ''[[...Baby One More Time (album)|...Baby One More Time]]'') and [[Rolling Stones|Stones]] ("[[(I Can't Get No) Satisfaction]]" on ''[[Oops!... I Did It Again (album)|Oops!... I Did It Again]]'') songs."<ref name="RSreview">{{cite magazine |author=Barry Walters | title=Britney|magazine=Rolling Stone |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/britney-252189/ |date=22 November 2001 |access-date=17 April 2022|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20070212133054/http://www.rollingstone.com/reviews/album/225846/britney |archive-date=12 February 2007}}</ref> Another positive reception came from ''[[PopMatters]]''' editor Nikki Tranter, who enjoyed that the song is "different from the average run-of-the-mill pop offering," and praised that "she does strange justice to the tune, vamping up her vocals and turning out something, that while silly and camp, is actually a fun listen."<ref>{{cite news|last=Tranter|first=Nikki|title=Britney Spears: Britney <PopMatters>|url=https://www.popmatters.com/pm/review/spearsbritney-britney|access-date=2 January 2012|newspaper=[[PopMatters]]|date=5 November 2001}}</ref> In contrast, David Browne wrote for ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]'' that "her remake is neither imaginative (it simply xeroxes Joan Jett's arrangement) nor all that believable."<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Browne |first1=David |title=Britney |url=https://ew.com/article/2001/11/12/britney/ |magazine=Entertainment Weekly |access-date=17 April 2022 |date=12 November 2001}}</ref>

sections.heading: Background
sections.wikitext: In December 2019, LadBaby announced his bid for the official Christmas number one. As with their last release "[[We Built This City#LadBaby version|We Built This City]]", all proceeds from the single went to [[The Trussell Trust]]. He said, "We were blown away by the support we received on our Christmas Number 1 single last year and how far that money has gone into changing the lives of families living in poverty across the UK. We're continually looking for ways we can support food bank charity the Trussell Trust further as the size of the problem still facing so many adults (and children) is huge and we ALL need to do whatever we can to say goodbye to poverty once and for all in the UK! If we can use our social media presence for good by singing about sausage rolls, giving people something to smile about and helping families eat this year, then why wouldn't we. Officially, the most unanticipated single of the decade...AGAIN!"<ref>{{cite web |last=Copsey |first=Rob |date=9 December 2019 |title=LadBaby announces 2019 bid for Christmas Number 1 |url=https://www.officialcharts.com/chart-news/ladbaby-announces-bid-for-2019-christmas-number-1-with-new-single-i-love-sausage-rolls__27944/ |access-date=4 January 2020 |website=Official Charts}}</ref>

sections.heading: Charts
sections.wikitext:
On 20 December 2019, the song entered the [[UK Singles Chart]] at number one, claiming the [[List of UK Singles Chart Christmas number ones|Christmas number one]] with 93,000 chart sales and with 85,000 of that total coming via downloads. It was also the fastest-selling download since Artists for Grenfell version of "[[Bridge over Troubled Water (song)|Bridge over Troubled Water]]" in June 2017. LadBaby became the third act to have two consecutive Christmas number one singles and the first to have two successive novelty Christmas number ones in the UK. After reaching number one, LadBaby said, "How have we done this again? It's the best feeling in the world – it's a Christmas miracle yet again! Thank you everybody for supporting us once again, and all for an amazing cause. It's going to the Trussell Trust – to the 14 million people living in poverty in the UK. Who doesn't love a sausage roll at Christmas?"{{cite web |last=Copsey |first=Rob |date=20 December 2019 |title=On a roll! LadBaby score second Official Christmas Number 1 |url=https://www.officialcharts.com/chart-news/ladbaby-score-second-official-christmas-number-1-with-i-love-sausage-rolls-its-a-christmas-miracle-again-__28042/ |access-date=4 January 2020 |website=Official Charts}} The song dropped from number one to number 57, and was overtaken by English singer [[Ellie Goulding]]'s cover of the [[Joni Mitchell]] song, "[[River (Joni Mitchell song)|River]]" (1971). {|class="wikitable sortable plainrowheaders" style="text-align:center" |- !
